L1119: ## Experimental API opt-in
L1120: 
L1121: Some app-server methods and fields are intentionally gated behind `experimentalApi` capability.
L1122:   * Omit `capabilities` (or set `experimentalApi` to `false`) to stay on the stable API surface, and the server rejects experimental methods/fields.
L1123:   * Set `capabilities.experimentalApi` to `true` to enable experimental methods and fields.

L1136:         }
L1137:       }
L1138:     }`
L1139: If a client sends an experimental method or field without opting in, app-server rejects it with:
L1140: 
L1141: `<descriptor> requires experimentalApi capability`
L1142: ## API overview
L1143:   * `thread/start` - create a new thread; emits `thread/started` and automatically subscribes you to turn/item events for that thread.
L1144:   * `thread/resume` - reopen an existing thread by id so later `turn/start` calls append to it.
L1145:   * `thread/fork` - fork a thread into a new thread id by copying stored history. Pass `lastTurnId` to copy history through that turn and omit later turns, or `ephemeral: true` to create an in-memory fork. Emits `thread/started` for the new thread; returned threads include `forkedFromId` when available.
L1146:   * `thread/read` - read a stored thread by id without resuming it; set `includeTurns` to return full turn history. Returned `thread` objects include runtime `status`.
L1147:   * `thread/list` - page through stored thread logs; supports cursor-based pagination plus `modelProviders`, `sourceKinds`, `archived`, `isPinned`, `cwd`, `useStateDbOnly`, `searchTerm`, and experimental `parentThreadId` or `ancestorThreadId` filters. Returned `thread` objects include runtime `status`.
L1148:   * `thread/turns/list` - experimental; page through a stored thread’s turn history without resuming it. `itemsView` controls whether turn items are omitted, summarized, or fully loaded.
L1149:   * `thread/items/list` - experimental; page through persisted thread items, optionally restricted to one `turnId`. The active thread store must support item pagination.
L1150:   * `thread/loaded/list` - list the thread ids currently loaded in memory.
L1151:   * `thread/name/set` - set or update a thread’s user-facing name for a loaded thread or a persisted rollout; emits `thread/name/updated`.
L1152:   * `thread/goal/set` - set the goal for a thread; emits `thread/goal/updated`.
L1153:   * `thread/goal/get` - read the current goal for a thread.
L1154:   * `thread/goal/clear` - clear the goal for a thread; emits `thread/goal/cleared`.
L1155:   * `thread/metadata/update` - patch SQLite-backed stored thread metadata, including persisted `gitInfo` and `isPinned`.
L1156:   * `thread/archive` - move a thread’s log file into the archived directory and attempt to archive spawned descendant thread logs that aren’t already archived; returns `{}` on success and emits `thread/archived` for each archived thread.
L1157:   * `thread/delete` - permanently delete a persisted active or archived thread and any spawned descendant threads; returns `{}` on success and emits `thread/deleted` for each deleted thread.
L1158:   * `thread/unsubscribe` - unsubscribe this connection from thread turn/item events. If this was the last subscriber, the server unloads the thread after a no-subscriber inactivity grace period and emits `thread/closed`.
L1159:   * `thread/unarchive` - restore an archived thread rollout back into the active sessions directory; returns the restored `thread` and emits `thread/unarchived`.
L1160:   * `thread/status/changed` - notification emitted when a loaded thread’s runtime `status` changes.
L1161:   * `thread/compact/start` - trigger conversation history compaction for a thread; returns `{}` immediately while progress streams via `turn/*` and `item/*` notifications.
L1162:   * `thread/shellCommand` - run a user-initiated shell command against a thread. This runs outside the sandbox with full access and doesn’t inherit the thread sandbox policy.
L1163:   * `thread/backgroundTerminals/clean` - stop all running background terminals for a thread (experimental; requires `capabilities.experimentalApi`).
L1164:   * `thread/backgroundTerminals/list` - list running background terminals for a loaded thread (experimental; requires `capabilities.experimentalApi`).

L905: 
L906:   * cite388†CLI customization L907:   * cite389†Developer commands L908:   * cite390†Developer settings L909: # Non-interactive mode
L910: 
L911: Use `codex exec` to run Codex in scripts and CI
L912: 
L913: Copy Page
L914: 
L915: Non-interactive mode lets you run Codex from scripts (for example, continuous integration (CI) jobs) without opening the interactive TUI. You invoke it with `codex exec`.
L916: 
L917: For flag-level details, see cite525†`codex exec` .
L918: ## When to use `codex exec`
L919: 
L920: Use `codex exec` when you want Codex to:
L921: 
L922:   * Run as part of a pipeline (CI, pre-merge checks, scheduled jobs).
L923:   * Produce output you can pipe into other tools (for example, to generate release notes or summaries).
L924:   * Fit naturally into CLI workflows that chain command output into Codex and pass Codex output to other tools.
L925:   * Run with explicit, pre-set sandbox and approval settings.
L926: ## Basic usage
L927: 
L928: Pass a task prompt as a single argument:
L929: 
L930:     `codex exec "summarize the repository structure and list the top 5 risky areas"`
L931: 
L932: While `codex exec` runs, Codex streams progress to `stderr` and prints only the final agent message to `stdout`. This makes it straightforward to redirect or pipe the final result:
L933: 
L934:     `codex exec "generate release notes for the last 10 commits" | tee release-notes.md`
L935: Use `--ephemeral` when you don’t want to persist session rollout files to disk:
L936: 
L937:     `codex exec --ephemeral "triage this repository and suggest next steps"`
L938: 
L939: If stdin is piped and you also provide a prompt argument, Codex treats the prompt as the instruction and the piped content as additional context.
L940: This lets you generate input with one command and hand it directly to Codex:
L941: 
L942:     `curl -s https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/comments \
L943:       | codex exec "format the top 20 items into a markdown table" \
L944:       > table.md`
L945: 
L946: For more advanced stdin piping patterns, see cite526†Advanced stdin piping .
L947: ## Permissions and safety
L948: 
L949: By default, `codex exec` runs in a read-only sandbox. In automation, set the least permissions needed for the workflow:
L950: 
L951:   * Allow edits: `codex exec --sandbox workspace-write "<task>"`
L952:   * Allow broader access: `codex exec --sandbox danger-full-access "<task>"`
L953: 
L954: Use `danger-full-access` only in a controlled environment (for example, an isolated CI runner or container).
L955: Codex keeps `codex exec --full-auto` as a deprecated compatibility flag and prints a warning. Prefer the explicit `--sandbox workspace-write` flag in new scripts.
L956: 
L957: Use `--ignore-user-config` when you need a run that doesn’t load `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`, and `--ignore-rules` when you need to skip user and project execpolicy `.rules` files for a controlled automation environment.
L958: If you configure an enabled MCP server with `required = true` and it fails to initialize, `codex exec` exits with an error instead of continuing without that server.
L959: ## Make output machine-readable
L960: 
L961: To consume Codex output in scripts, use JSON Lines output:
L962: 
L963:     `codex exec --json "summarize the repo structure" | jq`
L964: 
L965: When you enable `--json`, `stdout` becomes a JSON Lines (JSONL) stream so you can capture every event Codex emits while it’s running. Event types include `thread.started`, `turn.started`, `turn.completed`, `turn.failed`, `item.*`, and `error`.
L966: Item types include agent messages, reasoning, command executions, file changes, MCP tool calls, web searches, and plan updates.
L967: Sample JSON stream (each line is a JSON object):
L968: 
L969:     `{"type":"thread.started","thread_id":"0199a213-81c0-7800-8aa1-bbab2a035a53"}
L970:     {"type":"turn.started"}
L971:     {"type":"item.started","item":{"id":"item_1","type":"command_execution","command":"bash -lc ls","status":"in_progress"}}
L972:     {"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_3","type":"agent_message","text":"Repo contains docs, sdk, and examples directories."}}
L973:     {"type":"turn.completed","usage":{"input_tokens":24763,"cached_input_tokens":24448,"output_tokens":122,"reasoning_output_tokens":0}}`
L974: If you only need the final message, write it to a file with `-o <path>`/`--output-last-message <path>`. This writes the final message to the file and still prints it to `stdout` (see cite525†`codex exec` for details).
L975: ## Create structured outputs with a schema
L976: 
L977: If you need structured data for downstream steps, use `--output-schema` to request a final response that conforms to a JSON Schema. This is useful for automated workflows that need stable fields (for example, job summaries, risk reports, or release metadata).

L911: Give ChatGPT and Codex new capabilities and expertise
L912: 
L913: Copy Page
L914: 
L915: Use agent skills to extend ChatGPT and Codex with task-specific capabilities. A skill packages instructions, resources, and optional scripts so either product can follow a workflow reliably. Skills build on the cite525†open agent skills standard†agentskills.io .
L916: Skills are the authoring format for reusable workflows. Plugins distribute reusable skills and connectors through the universal plugin directory shared by ChatGPT and Codex. Plugins work in Chat and Work across ChatGPT on the web, desktop, and mobile, in Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app, and through Codex CLI. Use skills to design the workflow itself, then package it as a cite526†plugin†developers.openai.com when you want other people to install it.
L917: Standalone skills are available in the ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and IDE extension. Skills bundled in plugins are also available in Chat and Work across ChatGPT on the web, desktop, and mobile.
L918: 
L919: In the ChatGPT desktop app, open Skills in the sidebar to view and explore skills created across your projects.
L920: 
L921: Atlas Control (macOS)Use the bundled CLI to control Atlas and inspect local browser data.Personal
L922: Exec Plan Create, maintain, and execute long-form execution plans ("ExecPlans") for complex work.Personal
L923: 
L924: GitHub Fix CI Debug failing GitHub Actions CI Personal
L925: 
L926: Linear Manage Linear issues in Codex Personal
L927: 
L928: OpenAI Docs Reference the official OpenAI Developer docs Personal
L929: 
L930: Yeet Stage, commit, and open PR Personal
L931: 
L932: cite527†Image Skill Creator Create or update a skill System
L933: 
L934: Skill Installer Install curated skills from openai/skills or other repos System
L935: 
L936: $
L937: 
L938: 6 Sol Mediumcite528†Image cite529†Image L939: Skills use progressive disclosure to manage context efficiently. ChatGPT and Codex start with each skill’s name and description, then load the full `SKILL.md` instructions when they decide to use that skill.
L940: In Codex, the initial list also includes each skill’s file path. To avoid crowding out the rest of the prompt, this list uses at most 2% of the model’s context window, or 8,000 characters when the context window is unknown. If many skills are installed, Codex shortens skill descriptions first. For large skill sets, Codex may omit some skills from the initial list and show a warning.
L941: This budget applies only to the initial skills list. When Codex selects a skill, it still reads the full SKILL.md instructions for that skill.
L942: 
L943: A skill is a directory with a `SKILL.md` file plus optional scripts and references. The `SKILL.md` file must include `name` and `description`.
L944: 
L945:   * my-skill/
L946: 
L947:     * SKILL.md Required: instructions + metadata
L948: 
L949:     * scripts/ Optional: executable code
L950: 
L951:     * references/ Optional: documentation
L952: 
L953:     * assets/ Optional: templates, resources
L954: 
L955:     * agents/
L956:       * openai.yaml Optional: appearance and dependencies
L957: ## How ChatGPT and Codex use skills
L958: 
L959: ChatGPT and Codex can activate skills in two ways:
L960: 
L961:   1. Explicit invocation: Include the skill directly in your prompt. In ChatGPT, type `@` to select a skill. In Codex CLI or the IDE extension, run `/skills` or type `$` to mention a skill.
L962:   2. Implicit invocation: ChatGPT or Codex can choose a skill when your task matches the skill `description`.
L963: Because implicit matching depends on `description`, write concise descriptions with clear scope and boundaries. Front-load the key use case and trigger words so a host can still match the skill if descriptions are shortened.
L964: ## Create a skill
L965: 
L966: If you already know the workflow and it’s easier to show than describe, use cite364†Record & Replay . The recorder captures the workflow, inspects the steps, and drafts a reusable skill from the demonstration.
L967: 
L968: If you want to describe the skill instead, use the built-in creator. In ChatGPT Work, invoke it as `@skill-creator`. In Codex, invoke it as:
L969: 
L970:     `$skill-creator`
L971: The creator asks what the skill does, when it should trigger, and whether it should stay instruction-only or include scripts. Instruction-only is the default.
L972: 
L973: You can also create a skill manually by creating a folder with a `SKILL.md` file:
L974: 
L975:     `---
L976:     name: skill-name
L977:     description: Explain exactly when this skill should and should not trigger.
L978:     ---
L979: 
L980:     Skill instructions for ChatGPT or Codex to follow.`
L981: Codex detects skill changes automatically. If an update doesn’t appear, restart Codex.
L982: ## Where Codex loads local skills
L983: 
L984: Codex reads skills from repository, user, admin, and system locations. For repositories, Codex scans `.agents/skills` in every directory from your current working directory up to the repository root. If two skills share the same `name`, Codex doesn’t merge them; both can appear in skill selectors.
L985: Skill Scope  | Location  | Suggested use
L986: --- | --- | ---
L987: `REPO`  | `$CWD/.agents/skills`
L988: Current working directory: where you launch Codex.  | If you’re in a repository or code environment, teams can check in skills relevant to a working folder. For example, skills only relevant to a microservice or a module.
L989: `REPO`  | `$CWD/../.agents/skills`
L990: A folder above CWD when you launch Codex inside a Git repository.  | If you’re in a repository with nested folders, organizations can check in skills relevant to a shared area in a parent folder.
L991: `REPO`  | `$REPO_ROOT/.agents/skills`
L992: The topmost root folder when you launch Codex inside a Git repository.  | If you’re in a repository with nested folders, organizations can check in skills relevant to everyone using the repository. These serve as root skills available to any subfolder in the repository.
L993: `USER`  | `$HOME/.agents/skills`
L994: Any skills checked into the user’s personal folder.  | Use to curate skills relevant to a user that apply to any repository the user may work in.
L995: `ADMIN`  | `/etc/codex/skills`
L996: Any skills checked into the machine or container in a shared, system location.  | Use for SDK scripts, automation, and for checking in default admin skills available to each user on the machine.

L904: 
L905: Use subagents in ChatGPT and Codex, and configure custom Codex agents
L906: 
L907: cite525†Image ChatGPT desktop app
L908: 
L909: Copy Page
L910: 
L911: ChatGPT Work and Codex can run subagent workflows by spawning specialized agents in parallel and then collecting their results in one response. This can be particularly helpful for complex tasks that are highly parallel, such as codebase exploration or implementing a multi-step feature plan.
L912: In local Codex clients, you can also define custom agents with different model configurations and instructions for different tasks.
L913: ## Availability
L914: 
L915: ChatGPT Work exposes subagent workflows and activity to eligible accounts.
L916: 
L917: Current Codex releases enable subagent workflows by default. Subagent activity appears in the ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and the IDE extension.
L918: 
L919: Because each subagent does its own model and tool work, subagent workflows consume more tokens than comparable single-agent runs.
L920: In ChatGPT Work, ask ChatGPT to delegate independent work to subagents. The agents run in ChatGPT’s hosted environment, and the chat shows their activity and results. At most intelligence levels, ask for delegation explicitly. With Ultra, ChatGPT can proactively delegate work when parallel agents would materially improve speed or quality.
L921: Ask Codex in an app chat to delegate independent parts of the work to subagents. Current local Codex releases delegate when you ask directly or when applicable `AGENTS.md` or skill instructions request it. The app surfaces each subagent thread so you can inspect its work and the summary returned to the main chat.
L922: Ask Codex in an interactive CLI session to use subagents. Codex can also follow applicable `AGENTS.md` or skill instructions that request delegation. Use `/agent` to inspect and switch between agent threads while they run. The main thread collects the subagent results into its final response.
L923: Ask Codex in an IDE chat to delegate independent parts of the work to subagents. Codex can also follow applicable `AGENTS.md` or skill instructions that request delegation. When the background-agent UI is available, active subagents appear above the composer. Expand the panel to see their status, stop all active subagents, or open an individual subagent thread.
L924: ## Why subagent workflows help
L925: 
L926: Even with large context windows, models have limits. If you flood the main chat (where you’re defining requirements, constraints, and decisions) with noisy intermediate output such as exploration notes, test logs, stack traces, and command output, the session can become less reliable over time.
L927: 
L928: This is often described as:
L929:   * Context pollution: useful information gets buried under noisy intermediate output.
L930:   * Context rot: performance degrades as the chat fills up with less relevant details.
L931: 
L932: For background, see the Chroma writeup on cite526†context rot†research.trychroma.com .
L933: 
L934: Subagent workflows help by moving noisy work off the main thread:
L935:   * Keep the main agent focused on requirements, decisions, and final outputs.
L936:   * Run specialized subagents in parallel for exploration, tests, or log analysis.
L937:   * Return summaries from subagents instead of raw intermediate output.
L938: They can also save time when the work can run independently in parallel, and they make larger-shaped tasks more tractable by breaking them into bounded pieces. For example, Codex can split analysis of a multi-million-token document into smaller problems and return distilled takeaways to the main thread.
L939: As a starting point, use parallel agents for read-heavy tasks such as exploration, tests, triage, and summarization. Be more careful with parallel write-heavy workflows, because agents editing code at once can create conflicts and increase coordination overhead.
L940: ## Core terms
L941: 
L942: Codex uses a few related terms in subagent workflows:
L943: 
L944:   * Subagent workflow: A workflow where Codex runs parallel agents and combines their results.
L945:   * Subagent: A delegated agent that Codex starts to handle a specific task.
L946:   * Agent thread: The thread where a subagent does its work. Supported clients let you open these threads to inspect progress or results.
